newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Uzbek opposition welcomes human rights seminar.
newsitem.headline: Uzbek opposition welcomes human rights seminar.

text.p: Uzbek President Islam Karimov won a nod of approval on Friday from some of his fiercest critics for spearheading a new drive to defend human rights and hosting a three-day conference on the subject.

The seminar, organised by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and the Uzbek government, brought together representatives of international human rights organisations and specialists from 13 countries.

Uzbek opposition politicians and human rights campaigners, who have frequently accused the authorities of being intolerant of opposition groups, welcomed the forum as an opportunity to express their views and to air grievances.
Karimov, Uzbekistan's Communist Party boss in Soviet times, has ruled the largely desert nation of 23 million with a rod of iron since independence in 1991, intolerant of dissent.

Russia's Interfax news agency quoted opposition activist Shukrullo Mirsaidov, a former vice-president, as telling the seminar that he hoped "the wind of change blowing in Uzbekistan would not die down".

The meeting, which was due to end later on Friday, was marked by unprecedented interviews on state-controlled Uzbek Radio with opposition figures who praised signs of progress in human rights but said the country still had a long way to go.

Former political prisoner Inomzhon Tursunov told the radio, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, that the opposition should be constructive in its demands and cooperate with the government.
"Our democratic process is still very young -- only five years have passed since we gained independence," he said.

"It is not easy to change everything at one stroke, especially when it comes to human rights. It should be noted that the policy currently being pursued on protection of human rights is necessary and very appropriate."
Karimov, in an opening address to the seminar, said Uzbekistan was committed to defending human rights and building "an open democratic society".
He said institutions had to be strengthened to ensure that freedoms were protected and he supported cooperation with international human rights organisations.
